questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man in rural New Mexico presents in July with 2 days of high fever, chills and a very swollen, exquisitely tender lump in the right groin. His cat had been hunting prairie dogs and had fleas. Temperature is 39.9 C (103.8 F), and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Aspirate of the groin node shows small gram-negative rods that stain darker at both ends, like a safety pin.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Oral metronidazole
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly
Gentamicin or streptomycin
Supportive care alone
Atovaquone-proguanil

explain.html:
Fever with a massively swollen tender node (bubo) after flea exposure from a pet that hunts rodents in the western US, and bipolar safety-pin gram-negative rods in the node aspirate, identify bubonic plague from Yersinia pestis. Rodents are the reservoir and fleas carry it to humans, who can also be infected by handling infected animals.

All forms of plague have high mortality without treatment. Treatment is streptomycin or gentamicin, with doxycycline or fluoroquinolones as alternatives.
why: Metronidazole treats anaerobes and protozoa, not Y. pestis.
Penicillin is used for syphilis and leptospirosis, not plague.
Untreated plague has high mortality, so supportive care alone is wrong.
Atovaquone-proguanil is an antimalarial.
explain.takeaway: Yersinia pestis (rodent reservoir, flea vector, bipolar gram-negative rod) causes bubonic plague, treated with streptomycin or gentamicin.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old musician who makes his own drums from imported goat hides notices a painless, itchy papule on his forearm. Over 5 days it becomes a painless ulcer with a black, depressed center surrounded by marked nonpitting edema. A Gram stain of the lesion shows large gram-positive rods with square ends, some with central spores.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Local wound care only, since skin infection stays localized
Topical antibiotic ointment for 2 weeks
Surgical excision of the lesion without antibiotics
Antitoxin alone without antibiotics
Systemic ciprofloxacin, since the infection can disseminate

explain.html:
A painless papule progressing to a black eschar with surrounding edema in someone handling animal hides, plus large square-ended gram-positive spore-forming rods, is cutaneous anthrax from Bacillus anthracis. The skin is the usual portal; anthrax toxin produces the edema. Spores can survive for years in soil and animal products.

Bacteria can spread through lymphatics to severe illness and death, and about 20% of cutaneous cases disseminate, so cutaneous anthrax should always be treated with a systemic antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin is the slide treatment, with penicillin and doxycycline also used.
why: Cutaneous anthrax disseminates in about 20% of cases, so it is never left untreated.
Topical therapy does not prevent lymphatic spread.
Antibiotics are always needed; excision alone does not treat the infection.
Antibiotic therapy is the slide treatment.
explain.takeaway: Cutaneous anthrax (painless eschar with edema after animal hide contact) is always treated with a systemic antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin because of a 20% dissemination risk.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old mail sorter develops fever, malaise and a dry cough, followed 3 days later by severe dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension. Chest radiograph shows a markedly widened mediastinum and a left lower lobe consolidation. Blood cultures grow large aerobic gram-positive rods that form spores.

Which of the following best explains his chest radiograph findings?
choices: Spirochetes reaching the lungs after exposure to rat urine
Bacteria seeding the lung from a flea bite in the axilla
Intracellular bacteria inhaled from dust around the placenta of a farm animal
Spores inhaled and germinating with toxin-driven mediastinal hemorrhage
Bird-derived intracellular bacteria causing interstitial pneumonia

explain.html:
Large aerobic spore-forming gram-positive rods in the blood with a wide mediastinum identify inhalational anthrax, the form linked to the 2001 bioterrorism letters sent through the US mail.

Airborne exposure to Bacillus anthracis spores leads to pneumonia, mediastinal hemorrhage from toxin production, bloodstream infection and death. The widened mediastinum on the radiograph reflects that hemorrhage and edema.
why: Rat-urine spirochetes describe leptospirosis.
Flea-borne gram-negative rods describe plague, and they do not form spores.
Inhalation near animal birth describes Coxiella (Q fever), not a gram-positive rod.
Bird exposure with interstitial pneumonia describes psittacosis.
explain.takeaway: Inhalational anthrax (spores, often bioterrorism) causes pneumonia with mediastinal hemorrhage, seen as a widened mediastinum.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old woman who recently visited family in a village in Mexico has 6 weeks of fevers that come and go over days, night sweats, fatigue and low back pain. While there she ate fresh soft goat cheese made from unpasteurized milk. She has hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Blood cultures grow small gram-negative coccobacilli after prolonged incubation.

Which feature of this organism best explains her prolonged course?
choices: Production of a heat-stable toxin preformed in food
Survival within macrophages of the liver, spleen and marrow
Formation of spores that persist in soil for years
Invasion of red blood cells of all ages
Dormant hepatocyte forms that reactivate months later

explain.html:
Undulant fever, sweats, back pain, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy after eating unpasteurized goat cheese in Mexico describe brucellosis, most likely Brucella melitensis (goats and sheep, Mexico and the Mediterranean, more severe disease). There is no human-to-human spread.

The bacteria travel from the portal of entry to lymph nodes and bloodstream and survive for long periods in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, producing a chronic granulomatous infection with waxing and waning symptoms. Acute disease is diagnosed by blood, bone marrow or node culture, and treatment is doxycycline, streptomycin or TMP-SMX.
why: Preformed heat-stable toxin describes Staph aureus food poisoning.
Long-lived soil spores describe Bacillus anthracis.
Invading red cells of all ages describes P. falciparum.
Dormant liver forms describe P. vivax and P. ovale.
explain.takeaway: Brucella (unpasteurized dairy, livestock) persists in liver, spleen, marrow and nodes, causing undulant fever and chronic granulomatous infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man returns from a whitewater rafting trip in Costa Rica. A week later he develops fever, severe myalgias of the calves and headache that improve after several days. A few days after that he becomes jaundiced with reduced urine output and bleeding into the whites of both eyes.

Total bilirubin: 9.8 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2)
Creatinine: 4.1 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2)
Platelets: 52,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000)

How was this infection most likely acquired?
choices: Handling a pet parrot
Bite of an Ixodes tick
Inhaling dust near a birthing animal
Water contaminated with animal urine
Eating undercooked ground beef

explain.html:
A biphasic illness after freshwater sports, with a flu-like first phase followed by jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage and conjunctival bleeding, is leptospirosis progressing to Weil disease (5 to 10% of patients). The cause is Leptospira interrogans, a spirochete.

Infected animals, especially rodents and dogs, shed large numbers of organisms in urine, and the bacteria survive in wet environments. Humans are infected when contaminated water or food enters through a break in the skin or a mucous membrane, or is swallowed. Penicillin or doxycycline works if started early.
why: Parrots transmit Chlamydophila psittaci.
Ixodes ticks carry Lyme disease, Anaplasma and Babesia.
Inhaling dust near a birthing animal describes Q fever.
Undercooked ground beef is linked to E. coli O157:H7.
explain.takeaway: Leptospira interrogans is acquired from water contaminated with animal urine and causes a biphasic illness that can progress to Weil disease (jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage).
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman who breeds parakeets and cockatiels in her home develops fever, severe headache and a dry cough. Two of her birds recently became lethargic and died. Chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Her spleen is palpable. Routine sputum culture grows only normal flora.

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: A fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute and convalescent sera
Gram stain of the sputum showing many gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci
Culture of the sputum on chocolate agar for 48 hours
Thin blood smear for intraerythrocytic organisms
Darkfield microscopy of the sputum for spirochetes

explain.html:
Atypical interstitial pneumonia with splenomegaly in someone exposed to sick pet birds is psittacosis, caused by Chlamydophila psittaci, an obligate intracellular coccoid organism carried in the blood, feces and feathers of parrots and many other birds. Infection is by handling birds or inhaling aerosolized organisms; the bacteria enter the respiratory tract and spread to the liver and spleen.

It is rarely diagnosed unless the exposure is asked about. Diagnosis is serologic: a fourfold increase in titer by complement fixation between acute and convalescent sera. Treatment is doxycycline or a macrolide.
why: Gram-positive diplococci would suggest a typical bacterial pneumonia, not an obligate intracellular organism.
Obligate intracellular bacteria do not grow on routine agar.
Intraerythrocytic organisms on smear suggest malaria or Babesia.
Darkfield is used for spirochetes such as Treponema or Leptospira.
explain.takeaway: Chlamydophila psittaci (pet birds) causes atypical pneumonia with liver and spleen spread; diagnose by a fourfold titer rise on paired sera and treat with doxycycline or a macrolide.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 10-year-old boy has a 3-week history of a tender, enlarged lymph node in his left axilla. His family adopted a kitten 6 weeks ago, and he had a small crusted papule on his left hand a few weeks before the node enlarged. He is otherwise well. Blood cultures are negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Culture of an aspirate from the lymph node
Peripheral blood smear for morulae
Serology for Francisella tularensis
Lymph node aspirate stained for bipolar rods
Serology for Bartonella henselae

explain.html:
Regional lymphadenopathy draining the site of a scratch from a young cat is cat scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae, a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus with cats (and their fleas) as the reservoir.

Cat scratch disease is diagnosed by serology. Organisms may be seen on tissue, but cultures are not positive, unlike bacillary angiomatosis or endocarditis where blood culture is useful. There is no consensus that antibiotics change the course of cat scratch disease.
why: Bartonella cultures are not positive in cat scratch disease.
Morulae point to Anaplasma or Ehrlichia.
Tularemia can follow cat contact too, but it is not the classic picture of a kitten scratch with a regional node.
Bipolar safety-pin rods in a node aspirate suggest plague.
explain.takeaway: Bartonella henselae from cats causes regional lymphadenopathy (cat scratch disease), diagnosed by serology because cultures are negative.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man who has been living in a crowded shelter with body lice has recurrent bouts of fever lasting several days, with leg pain and headache. Blood cultures are positive for a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus from a genus that also causes cat scratch disease. Public health officials note that, unlike its relatives, this species has no animal reservoir.

Which of the following illnesses is this organism classically known for?
choices: Oroya fever followed by verruga peruana
Trench fever
Rickettsialpox
Relapsing fever from Borrelia
Epidemic typhus from Rickettsia

explain.html:
A Bartonella species carried by lice with no animal reservoir is Bartonella quintana, the cause of trench fever (World War I). It also causes bacillary angiomatosis, bacteremia and endocarditis in people with HIV or other immunocompromise.

The other Bartonella species differ by vector and reservoir: B. bacilliformis is spread by sandflies in the Andes and causes Oroya fever (fever with hemolytic anemia) and later verruga peruana, while B. henselae lives in cats and their fleas.
why: Oroya fever and verruga peruana come from sandfly-borne B. bacilliformis in the Andes.
Rickettsialpox is caused by mite-borne R. akari.
Relapsing fever is a Borrelia illness, a different genus.
Epidemic typhus is louse-borne but caused by R. prowazekii, not Bartonella.
explain.takeaway: Bartonella quintana (body lice, no animal reservoir) causes trench fever; B. bacilliformis (sandflies, Andes) causes Oroya fever; B. henselae (cats) causes cat scratch disease.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old field biologist who traps ground squirrels in the western US is hospitalized with fever, cough productive of bloody sputum and rapidly worsening hypoxemia. Sputum Giemsa stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli with bipolar staining. Several days earlier she had a painful swollen axillary node.

Which of the following precautions is most important for staff caring for her?
choices: Contact precautions for draining wounds only
Avoiding shared food and water containers
Standard precautions only, since no human spread occurs
Respiratory isolation for airborne droplet spread
Protection from mosquito bites on the ward

explain.html:
A trapper of western ground squirrels with a prior painful axillary bubo, now with severe bloody bronchopneumonia and bipolar gram-negative coccobacilli in sputum, has Yersinia pestis infection that has progressed to pneumonic plague.

Plague is usually not spread person to person, but the pneumonic form can spread through the air. Prevention therefore includes isolation and quarantine, along with rodent control, chemoprophylaxis of contacts and vaccine.
why: Draining-wound precautions alone miss the airborne risk of pneumonic plague.
Plague is not a food or water-borne infection.
Most forms are not spread between people, but pneumonic plague can be.
Fleas, not mosquitoes, transmit plague.
explain.takeaway: Plague is usually not spread between humans, but pneumonic plague can spread through the air and requires isolation.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old landscaper on an island off Massachusetts presents in August with 4 days of fever, chills, dry cough and pleuritic chest pain. He mows large commercial lawns and recently ran over a rabbit nest. Chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe infiltrate with hilar adenopathy. Routine sputum and blood cultures are negative at 48 hours.

Which of the following is the most appropriate step regarding laboratory testing?
choices: Request a Wright stain of blood for morulae
Report the blood cultures as final negatives at 48 hours
Send serology and warn the laboratory before any culture
Order a thin and thick smear of the blood
Request a darkfield exam of the sputum

explain.html:
Pneumonia in a landscaper after mowing over a rabbit nest is classic pneumonic tularemia from Francisella tularensis, a tiny fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus that lives inside macrophages. Rabbits and hares (lagomorphs) are the reservoir; people are infected by skin contact with an infected animal, inhalation or a tick bite.

Diagnosis is usually serologic. It can be cultured on chocolate agar or BCYE, but the laboratory must be warned because handling the organism carries a high risk of lab infection. Blood cultures usually take more than 5 days to turn positive, so negative results at 48 hours mean little. Treatment is streptomycin or gentamicin.
why: Morulae point to Anaplasma or Ehrlichia.
F. tularensis blood cultures usually take more than 5 days, so 48 hours is too early.
Blood smears look for malaria or Babesia.
Darkfield is used to see spirochetes such as T. pallidum.
explain.takeaway: Tularemia (rabbits, lawn mowing, ticks) is diagnosed mainly by serology; warn the lab before culture because F. tularensis readily infects lab staff.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Four men develop fever, severe headache and dry cough about 2 weeks after a weekly card game held in a garage where a cat had given birth to kittens. Chest radiographs show bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Aminotransferases are mildly elevated, and a liver biopsy in one man shows granulomas. Routine bacterial cultures are negative.

Which long-term complication is this organism known for?
choices: Megacolon
Nephrotic syndrome
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Tabes dorsalis with locomotor ataxia
Culture-negative endocarditis

explain.html:
A cluster of atypical, bilateral pneumonia with granulomatous hepatitis after inhaling dust where an animal gave birth is Q fever, from Coxiella burnetii. The organism is concentrated in the placenta, resists drying, heat and sunlight, and is inhaled from the environment; it can also be swallowed in unpasteurized milk or cheese. It is not grown by usual culture methods.

Acute illness often resolves, but some cases become chronic and cause culture-negative endocarditis or osteomyelitis. Diagnosis is PCR early and serology after a week; acute disease is treated with a tetracycline and chronic disease with combination therapy.
why: Megacolon is a chronic complication of Chagas disease.
Nephrotic syndrome is a complication of P. malariae.
HUS follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
Tabes dorsalis is late neurosyphilis.
explain.takeaway: Coxiella burnetii (inhaled near animal births) causes atypical pneumonia and granulomatous hepatitis, and chronic Q fever causes culture-negative endocarditis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes tacrolimus and prednisone develops several red-purple, raised, vascular-appearing skin nodules on his arms and trunk, plus fever. Imaging shows multiple blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver. He has two cats at home and has had flea bites. Biopsy of a skin nodule shows proliferating small blood vessels with clumps of bacilli on silver stain.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Benznidazole
Intravenous artesunate
Doxycycline or a macrolide
No antibiotics; the illness is self-limited
Metronidazole

explain.html:
Vascular proliferative skin nodules and blood-filled liver lesions (peliosis hepatis) in an immunocompromised patient with cat and flea exposure are bacillary angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae (B. quintana can do the same). Blood culture may be positive, and skin or node tissue can be cultured.

Bacillary angiomatosis and Bartonella endocarditis are treated with doxycycline or a macrolide. Only cat scratch disease in a healthy host lacks consensus on antibiotics.
why: Benznidazole is for Chagas disease.
Artesunate is for severe malaria.
Unlike cat scratch disease, bacillary angiomatosis is treated.
Metronidazole treats anaerobes and protozoa.
explain.takeaway: Bacillary angiomatosis (vascular skin nodules, peliosis hepatis) in immunocompromised hosts is caused by Bartonella and treated with doxycycline or a macrolide.
explain.subject: Microbiology
